transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jon (Redwood SE), Priya (Zenith EM), Liam (Zenith CTO), Diego (Zenith DevOps), Hannah (Product)

--- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) ---
Customer wants to integrate Redwood into their existing LLM pipelines which use LangChain and LlamaIndex. Main concerns: data residency, VPC proxy for outbound requests, per-team rate limits, embedding pipeline throughput, and observability hooks for token-level latency and cost at route-level.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes, so we'll do a quick intro then dig into integration specifics, SDKs, and gateway requirements. Priya, do you want to kick with current stack?
[00:10] Priya: Sure, yeah. So we're a fintech, we run a microservice architecture. For LLM stuff we have a couple of services that use LangChain and LlamaIndex for RAG, retrieval, etc. Right now embeddings and generation are via another vendor but cost is high and latency spikes during batch jobs. We're evaluating Redwood because of the performance and the Dedicated offering for predictable throughput.
[00:30] Maya: thanks. quick question, are you using the LangChain python layers or more of a node sdk?
[00:35] Priya: Primarily Python. LangChain in Python, LlamaIndex for document indexes. Some teams use node but it's smaller.
[00:42] Alex: good, that helps. Maya is our SE who focuses on integration — she'll cover SDKs, connector patterns, and what we recommend for gateway/proxy setups.
[00:52] Maya: hi all. Overview: Redwood has official Python and Node SDKs. We also provide a LangChain integration guide and a LlamaIndex example repo. For python LangChain, it's basically a drop-in with a small adapter. There can be nuance with streaming vs non-streaming calls and how you manage the KV cache.
[01:10] Liam: when you say adapter, do we need to rewrite chains or is it wrapper-level?
[01:15] Maya: wrapper-level 99% of cases — you swap in the Redwood client and map the calls. For RAG we recommend using our embeddings endpoint for vector generation then store in your existing index. The LlamaIndex example handles chunking and metadata mapping.
[01:34] Priya: ok. on the infra side — we need to place a gateway/proxy in front because of egress rules and to centralize rate limiting per-team. Is that a pattern you see? What about tokenization/streaming compatibility?
[01:50] Jon: yes, totally common. Two patterns: 1) Redwood hosted API behind an internal gateway/proxy (we see customers run envoy or nginx to apply auth and per-team quotas). 2) For Dedicated/Private, you can run a customer-managed ingress in the VPC so requests never hit public internet. Both support streaming; for streaming via proxy you need to ensure the proxy preserves chunked transfer and SSE (server-sent events) if using our streaming APIs.
[02:18] Diego: if we put a proxy, can we also do per-route observability? we want token-level cost at route level and tracing hooks to correlate with our spans.
[02:29] Maya: yes — we emit request-level metadata in headers and tracing hooks. We have an observability webhooks feature and a tracing integration for open-telemetry. Typical pattern: your gateway injects X-Request-Id and we return token counts and latency in response headers or via post-call webhooks, then you can correlate. There's also per-route dashboards in the console.
[02:55] Hannah: are those headers consistent across Hosted and Dedicated?
[03:00] Maya: yes, same interface. On Private you have extra control — you can push logs directly to your S3 or SIEM and we can enable enhanced retention.
[03:12] Liam: what's the rate limiting model? we have a few teams with bursty traffic and another batch job for daily reindexing. We can't have burst jobs starving interactive flows.
[03:24] Alex: good q. We support quotas at org, workspace, api-key, and route levels. You can create a token bucket for interactive routes with low latency SLO and separate rate-limited batch routes with higher concurrency but lower priority. For Dedicated you can carve out reserved GPU capacity for critical routes.
[03:44] Priya: does that need separate API keys or can we do routing rules based on headers?
[03:50] Jon: both. Many customers create api keys per-service and then create routing policy rules. You can also route by header or path if you want to keep single key.
[03:58] Diego: and how are quotas enforced — at gateway or at runtime? we need enforcement even if the gateway misbehaves.
[04:05] Maya: quotas are enforced server-side in our control plane and at the runtime layer; the proxy is only advisory. So even if someone bypasses the gateway, the control plane will reject excess tokens.
[04:17] Liam: good. about data residency and encryption — if we go Dedicated vs Private what are the differences for KMS and audit logs?
[04:27] Alex: Hosted has customer-managed KMS integration for encryption at rest via bring-your-own-key in select plans; Dedicated and Private give you full control — in Private deployments the control plane can be in your VPC and keys never leave your account. Audit logs are available for all tiers, but Private can stream logs directly to your SIEM. We'll share the SOC2/ISO doc after this call.
[04:48] Priya: sweet. on the SDK side, we have a lot of existing code calling embeddings endpoints in parallel. Any guidance around batching to limit costs without hurting latency?
[05:00] Maya: yes — Redwood Optimize can run suggestions, but at integration time we recommend using client-side batching with our batching window, and prefix caching for repeat requests. For embeddings we recommend batching up to N based on your sequence length — we can help run a simulation with your typical lengths.
[05:20] Priya: N meaning tokens or number of items?
[05:22] Maya: number of items — depends on model and quantization. We'll benchmark with your data set.
[05:27] Liam: oops quick question on LlamaIndex — our indexes are large and retrievals are heavy. Does Redwood have any special support for vector stores or is it transparent?
[05:40] Jon: transparent — we don't host your indexes, you continue to serve them. We optimize the embedding generation path and recommend async embedding ingestion to your vector DB. For high-throughput ingestion we recommend Dedicated with burst capacity.
[05:58] Priya: about telemetry: Can you push token-level billing events into our telemetry pipeline? We want to break down cost per feature.
[06:10] Maya: yes — you can forward usage events to your billing pipeline using event webhooks or export via our console CSV. For real-time you can stream events to your Kafka or S3 in Private deployments.
[06:24] Hannah: wanted to ask about security review process — we'll have InfoSec ask for penetration test results and some compliance artifacts. How do we engage?
[06:32] Alex: typical path — we send the security pack (SOC2, pen test summary, architecture docs). For Dedicated/Private there's an architecture review with our solutions engineering and security. We'll also provide a checklist for the VPC setup and recommended IAM roles.
[06:48] Priya: good. can you also confirm SDK license? we're sensitive to any copyleft.
[06:54] Maya: our SDKs are permissive MIT. Example repos for LangChain/LlamaIndex are under MIT too.
[07:00] Liam: about latency SLOs — what sort of p95 numbers can we expect for generation for your hosted models vs dedicated?
[07:09] Jon: depends on model and sequence length. For our curated small-medium models hosted p95 for short prompts is in the 60-120ms range on average; for larger models it rises. On Dedicated with pinned GPUs and optimized kernels you can see more consistent p95 and lower tail latencies, especially with KV cache warmed and continuous batching tuned to your workload. We can run a benchmark with your prompt set to get exact numbers.
[07:36] Priya: that benchmark would be great — looking for p95 < 400ms for the interactive flows and throughput for batch jobs overnight.
[07:44] Alex: we'll include that in the action items.
[07:48] Diego: quick ops question — how does model rollout/versions work? if we pin a model and you push a security patch do we need to coordinate?
[07:58] Maya: rollouts are controlled — you pin versions or configure canary/A-B rollouts. For Dedicated we can schedule maintenance windows. We notify via webhooks and console alerts. Critical security patches are coordinated with the customer.
[08:13] Priya: about cost modeling: do you have a cost estimator for mixing streaming responses vs non-streaming? token accounting sometimes differs across vendors and it's hard to forecast.
[08:25] Alex: yes, we provide token-level cost breakdowns in the console and an estimator spreadsheet we'll send. For streaming vs non-streaming, cost accounting is based on tokens generated and consumed; streaming doesn't materially change billing but can change perceived latency and UX.
[08:44] Liam: any gotchas with LangChain chains that use function calling or tool calls?
[08:50] Maya: function calling is supported; you just map the function schema. One gotcha is batched tool calls — ensure your orchestration handles per-call context and you don't accidentally merge contexts across calls. We have examples in the repo.
[09:06] Hannah: do you have any example of a gateway config — like envoy or apisix — for preserving SSE?
[09:12] Jon: yes we have sample envoy and nginx configs. We'll share links. Main point: preserve chunked transfer encoding and don't buffer streaming responses.
[09:22] Priya: ok, on Dedicated vs Private — we're leaning Dedicated because we want Redwood-managed infra but predictable throughput. But we have strict egress controls and want to ensure no customer data leaves our VPC for Private vs Dedicated. what's the boundary?
[09:38] Alex: Dedicated is still managed by Redwood but you get reserved capacity isolated for your tenant; egress may transit Redwood control plane but we support customer-managed KMS and network isolation options. Private places everything in your VPC/on-prem, so nothing traverses Redwood public control plane. We can diagram both for you.
[09:58] Diego: for Dedicated, can we still use our internal proxy so requests never go outbound?
[10:04] Maya: yes — you can front Redwood with your proxy and we support mTLS to secure the connection; for sensitive flows many customers use private network links or dedicated peering.
[10:14] Priya: are there any constraints on embedding model sizes or quantized models we should know when we push to Dedicated?
[10:22] Jon: workload dependent. For quantized models we recommend certain runtimes; Dedicated supports common quantization profiles, but we'll advise based on model architecture. We'll run compatibility checks as part of onboarding.
[10:34] Liam: ok last technical: observability hooks — you said open-telemetry integration. Is there a sample span schema? we want to correlate with our trace ids.
[10:44] Maya: yes — we accept parent trace ids via headers and return Redwood span ids. We have a sample OTLP exporter and schema in the docs. We'll share the example.
[10:56] Alex: sound like we have good alignment. quick recap of next steps before we close?
[11:02] Priya: yes please. If you can run the benchmark with our prompts and give a Dedicated sizing estimate that'd be ideal. Also send security pack and pricing.
[11:10] Alex: action items again: Maya runs benchmark, Alex shares pricing and contract template, Diego to send traffic profile. We'll schedule the deep technical session July 22. Anything else?
[11:20] Hannah: that's it from product. Thanks everyone.
[11:24] Alex: thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[End of transcript]
